lesson.intro: Binary search is easy to describe and famously easy to get wrong. Think like strong candidates: a monotonic yes or no question, an invariant you keep true, and a range that shrinks every step, from sorted arrays to rotated ones to searching the answer.
objectives: Spot binary search problems from a monotonic yes or no question
Write the inclusive and half-open templates from their invariants
Pair the loop condition, mid rounding and updates so loops end

sections.title: When to reach for binary search
sections.key: Binary search needs a yes or no question with monotonic answers, all no then all yes. Each step halves the range, so a billion items take about 30 steps.
sections.body:
Guess my number between 1 and 1,000,000, asking only "is it bigger than x?". Ask about the middle and discard half each time: at most 20 questions, since 2^20 is just over a million. That is **binary search**, O(log n) instead of O(n).

It works whenever a yes or no question has **monotonic** answers: all no on one side, all yes on the other.

[[visual]]

- Find a value, or its insert position, in a sorted array.
- Find the first or last occurrence among duplicates.
- Find the minimum of a rotated sorted array.
- Find the smallest feasible speed or capacity: **binary search on the answer**, with no array at all.

Signals: "sorted", "rotated", "first" or "last", "minimum value such that", values up to 10^9.

[[visual 2]]

visual.title: A monotonic question, target 7
visual.caption: One probe in the middle tells you which side holds the switch, so the other half is discarded.

sections.deeper: **Why invariants?** The algorithm is short but has a reputation for off-by-one bugs. Jon Bentley reported that most professional programmers in his courses could not write a correct binary search, and a midpoint overflow bug sat in Java's standard library for years before it was found in 2006. The cure is not memorizing code but reasoning with an **invariant**, which the next sections teach.

activity.title: Halve the range
activity.prompt: Find the target in as few probes as you can. Before each probe, say which half you will throw away and why. Notice that 32 items never need more than 6 probes.

check.question: About how many steps does binary search need, at most, for 1,000,000 sorted items?
check.explanation: Each step halves the range, and 2^20 is about a million, so about 20 halvings reach a single item. 500,000 is the average for a linear scan.

sections.title: The inclusive template: lo <= hi
sections.key: Invariant: if the target exists, it is in `nums[lo..hi]`. Loop while `lo <= hi` and step past mid with `lo = mid + 1` or `hi = mid - 1`.
sections.body:
Every line of the classic exact search follows from that **invariant**, with both ends inclusive:

- Start with `lo = 0` and `hi = len(nums) - 1`: the whole array.
- Loop `while lo <= hi`: at least one element is left.
- Found: return mid. Too small: `lo = mid + 1`. Too big: `hi = mid - 1`. Both skip mid, so the range always shrinks.
- `lo > hi` means the range is empty: return -1.

[[visual]]

**Safe midpoint.** With fixed-size integers (Java, C++), `lo + hi` can overflow and turn negative. Write `mid = lo + (hi - lo) // 2`. Python never overflows, but the safe form is free.

Mid must be a whole number: plain `/` gives a fraction in Python 3 and JavaScript, and `nums[1.5]` is `undefined` in JavaScript.
sections.code:
def binary_search(nums, target):
    lo, hi = 0, len(nums) - 1        # if present, target is in nums[lo..hi]
    while lo <= hi:                  # the range holds at least one element
        mid = lo + (hi - lo) // 2    # overflow-safe, rounds down
        if nums[mid] == target:
            return mid
        if nums[mid] < target:
            lo = mid + 1             # target can only be right of mid
        else:
            hi = mid - 1             # target can only be left of mid
    return -1                        # empty range: not present

nums = [1, 3, 5, 7, 9, 11, 13]
print(binary_search(nums, 9))    # 4
print(binary_search(nums, 4))    # -1
print(binary_search([], 4))      # -1
sections.pitfall: Writing `lo = mid` or `hi = mid` in this template. With `lo <= hi`, a one-element range has lo == hi == mid, so `lo = mid` changes nothing and the loop never ends. Both updates must step past mid.

check.question: In the inclusive template, why does the loop run while lo <= hi rather than while lo < hi?
choices: lo can never equal hi in this template
To avoid integer overflow when computing mid
So the loop always runs one extra time for safety
When lo == hi the range still holds one element, which must be checked
check.explanation: [lo, hi] is inclusive, so lo == hi means one candidate is left. With lo < hi the loop would stop before checking it and miss a target in that last position.

sections.title: The half-open template and lower bound
sections.key: Lower bound finds the first index with `nums[i] >= target`: start `hi = len(nums)`, loop while `lo < hi`, set `lo = mid + 1` or `hi = mid`, and return lo.
sections.body:
Often the question is not "where is the target?" but "where is the first element at least the target?". That **lower bound** is the insert position, the first occurrence among duplicates, and the count of smaller elements.

Use a **half-open** range `[lo, hi)` with this invariant: everything before `lo` is less than the target, and everything from `hi` on is at least the target.

[[visual]]

Why doesn't `hi = mid` loop forever? Mid rounds down and `lo < hi`, so mid < hi and the range still shrinks.

[[visual 2]]

Python ships this as `bisect.bisect_left`. `bisect_right` returns the first position greater than the target, so `bisect_right - bisect_left` counts the copies, and `bisect_right - 1` is the last occurrence when present.

steps.label: Set lo = 0 and hi = len(nums)
steps.detail: n, not n - 1: the answer may be past the end

steps.label: Is nums[mid] < target?
steps.yes: lo = mid + 1: mid and everything left of it are too small
steps.no: hi = mid: mid might be the answer, so keep it

sections.code:
import bisect

def lower_bound(nums, target):
    lo, hi = 0, len(nums)            # half-open: the answer is in [lo, hi]
    while lo < hi:
        mid = lo + (hi - lo) // 2
        if nums[mid] < target:
            lo = mid + 1             # mid and everything left are too small
        else:
            hi = mid                 # mid might be the answer: keep it
    return lo

nums = [1, 3, 3, 3, 5, 6]
print(lower_bound(nums, 3), bisect.bisect_left(nums, 3))   # 1 1
print(bisect.bisect_right(nums, 3))                        # 4
print(lower_bound(nums, 7))                                # 6
sections.pitfall: Starting the half-open template with `hi = len(nums) - 1`. The answer "after the end" becomes impossible, so a value larger than everything returns the last index instead of n.

check.question: What does lower_bound([2, 4, 4, 8], 5) return?
check.explanation: The first element that is at least 5 is 8, at index 3. That is also where 5 would be inserted to keep the array sorted. Lower bound never returns -1; when nothing qualifies it returns len(nums).

sections.title: Avoiding infinite loops
sections.key: Every iteration must shrink the range: if you write `lo = mid`, round mid up; if you write `hi = mid`, round mid down.
sections.body:
You want the **last** index whose value is at most the target, so you write `lo = mid` when `nums[mid] <= target` and `hi = mid - 1` otherwise. On `[1, 2]` with target 5: lo = 0, hi = 1, mid = 0, so lo = 0. Nothing changed, forever.

Check the two-element case, where rounding bites:

- `lo + (hi - lo) // 2` rounds **down**, so mid == lo: `lo = mid` is stuck, while `hi = mid` makes progress.
- `lo + (hi - lo + 1) // 2` rounds **up**, so mid == hi: `hi = mid` is stuck, while `lo = mid` makes progress.

[[visual]]

Two habits make these reliable:

- Write the invariant as a comment before the loop; every update must keep it true.
- Trace arrays of length 0, 1 and 2, with the target below everything, above everything and absent.

In production, use `bisect`; in interviews, derive the loop from the invariant.

visual.title: The three safe templates
rows: `lo = mid + 1` or `hi = mid - 1`; ends with lo > hi when absent
First index where cond is true (F F T T)
`hi = mid` when true, else `lo = mid + 1`; ends at lo == hi
Last index where cond is true (T T F F)
`lo = mid` when true, else `hi = mid - 1`; ends at lo == hi

sections.pitfall: Pairing `lo = mid` with a mid that rounds down. On a two-element range mid equals lo, nothing changes and the loop never ends. Round up whenever an update keeps mid on the low side.

activity.title: Unstick the loop
activity.prompt: The first call gets stuck (a step counter stops it after 10 rounds). Trace it by hand on [1, 2], then change one line using the pairing rule from this section.

props.task: Change how mid is computed so the first call prints 1 and the second still prints 2.

check.question: lo = 3 and hi = 4. With mid rounding down, what is mid, and what happens if the code sets lo = mid?
choices: mid = 3.5, which is not a valid index
mid = 3, and lo stays 3, so the loop makes no progress and repeats forever
check.explanation: 3 + (4 - 3) // 2 = 3, so lo = mid assigns 3 to lo again. The range never shrinks. Rounding up gives mid = 4, and lo = mid then moves forward.

sections.title: Rotated sorted arrays
sections.key: In a rotated sorted array at least one half around mid is always sorted, and comparing with an endpoint tells you which, so O(log n) search still works.
sections.body:
Rotate `[0, 1, 2, 4, 5, 6, 7]` into `[4, 5, 6, 7, 0, 1, 2]`: two sorted runs. Binary search still works, because **at least one half around any mid is sorted**.

**Minimum** (the "first true" template): if `nums[mid] > nums[hi]`, the drop is right of mid, so `lo = mid + 1`; otherwise mid..hi is sorted, so `hi = mid`.

[[visual]]

**Search for a target** with the inclusive template: find the sorted half, then check whether the target lies in it.

[[visual 2]]

Both are O(log n) for **distinct** values. With duplicates like `[1, 1, 1, 0, 1]`, equal ends hide the sorted half: O(n) worst case.

visual.title: Finding the minimum
visual.caption: Comparing with `nums[hi]`, not `nums[lo]`, also handles an array that was never rotated, with no special case.

items.title: `nums[lo] <= nums[mid]`
points: Go left (`hi = mid - 1`) when `nums[lo] <= target < nums[mid]`

items.title: Otherwise
points: Go right (`lo = mid + 1`) when `nums[mid] < target <= nums[hi]`

sections.code:
def find_min(nums):                   # rotated, distinct values
    lo, hi = 0, len(nums) - 1
    while lo < hi:
        mid = lo + (hi - lo) // 2
        if nums[mid] > nums[hi]:
            lo = mid + 1      # the drop is to the right of mid
        else:
            hi = mid          # mid..hi sorted: minimum at mid or left
    return nums[lo]

print(find_min([4, 5, 6, 7, 0, 1, 2]))   # 0
print(find_min([11, 13, 15, 17]))        # 11  (not rotated)
print(find_min([2, 1]))                  # 1
sections.deeper:
**Target 0 in `[4, 5, 6, 7, 0, 1, 2]`.** lo = 0, hi = 6, mid = 3 (7). The left half 4 to 7 is sorted and 0 is not in [4, 7), so lo = 4. Now mid = 5 (1). The left half, indexes 4 to 5 with values 0 to 1, is sorted and 0 is in [0, 1), so hi = 4. mid = 4: found at index 4.

**Why duplicates hurt.** When `nums[lo]`, `nums[mid]` and `nums[hi]` are all equal, either half could hold the drop, so the safe move is to shrink the range by one.
sections.pitfall: Writing `nums[lo] < nums[mid]` instead of `<=` to test whether the left half is sorted. When lo == mid the left half is one sorted element; with `<` the code throws the target away, as `[3, 1]` with target 1 shows.

check.question: In [5, 6, 7, 1, 2, 3, 4], mid is index 3 (value 1) and hi is index 6 (value 4). Where is the minimum?
choices: Strictly to the right of mid
At mid or to its left, because nums[mid] <= nums[hi] means mid..hi is sorted
It cannot be decided without scanning the array
check.explanation: 1 <= 4, so indexes 3 to 6 are in sorted order and nothing right of mid is smaller than nums[mid]. The search continues with hi = mid, and here mid itself holds the minimum.

sections.title: Binary search on the answer
sections.key: When "does x work?" is monotonic, binary search the range of possible answers for the first x that works, running a feasibility check at each probe.
sections.body:
A printer has jobs of `[3, 6, 7, 11]` pages and 8 hours. Each hour it prints up to s pages of one job, idling if that job finishes early. What is the slowest speed s that finishes in time?

No sorted array, but a monotonic question: can we finish at speed s? If s works, every faster speed works.

[[visual]]

[[visual 2]]

Each check is O(n), with O(log M) checks for a largest job of M pages: O(n log M), versus O(n M) for trying every speed.

Use integer ceilings, `(p + s - 1) // s`; floats can misround huge values.

steps.label: Bound the answer
steps.detail: Speed 1 up to the largest job, 11, which surely works when there are at least as many hours as jobs

steps.label: Write the yes or no check
steps.detail: feasible(s): the sum of ceil(pages / s) is at most 8

steps.label: Find the first feasible value
steps.detail: lo < hi, hi = mid when feasible, else lo = mid + 1

visual.title: Jobs [3, 6, 7, 11], 8 hours, speeds 1 to 11
visual.caption: lo == hi == 4, so the minimum speed is 4.

sections.code:
def first_true(lo, hi, feasible):      # feasible must be monotonic
    while lo < hi:
        mid = lo + (hi - lo) // 2
        if feasible(mid):
            hi = mid          # mid works: the answer is mid or smaller
        else:
            lo = mid + 1      # mid fails: the answer is larger
    return lo

def hours_needed(jobs, speed):
    return sum((p + speed - 1) // speed for p in jobs)   # integer ceiling

jobs = [3, 6, 7, 11]
print(first_true(1, max(jobs), lambda s: hours_needed(jobs, s) <= 8))  # 4

def isqrt(n):                          # largest r with r * r <= n
    return first_true(0, n + 1, lambda r: r * r > n) - 1

print(isqrt(17), isqrt(16), isqrt(0))  # 4 4 0
sections.deeper: **The same shape appears everywhere:** the smallest ship capacity that delivers all packages within D days, splitting an array into k parts to minimize the largest sum, the integer square root, the first day on which enough flowers have bloomed. The skill is noticing the monotonic yes or no question hiding in the problem.
sections.pitfall: Searching a range that does not contain the answer, or using a predicate that is not monotonic. Pick hi so it surely works, and check that "x works" really implies "every larger x works".

check.question: Why can the minimum printing speed be found with binary search even though no sorted array is given?
choices: Feasibility is monotonic: if speed s works, every faster speed works too
Every problem about integers can be binary searched
Each job takes exactly one hour
check.explanation: Binary search needs answers that switch from no to yes once. Faster printing never needs more hours, so the feasible speeds form one block starting at the answer. The jobs need not be sorted.

sections.title: Practice: choosing a template and testing it
sections.key: Name the question, state the invariant, pick the matching template and rounding, set bounds that include every answer, then test tiny inputs.
sections.body:
Before you type, work through five steps:

[[visual]]

Common bugs:

- Mixing templates: `lo < hi` with `hi = mid - 1` where `hi = mid` was needed, or `lo <= hi` with `hi = mid`.
- `lo = mid` with a mid that rounds down: an infinite loop on two elements.
- `hi = len(nums) - 1` when the answer can be past the end.
- `(lo + hi) / 2` without rounding, or overflowing in fixed-width languages.
- Rotated-array search with duplicates, still claiming O(log n).

Array templates are O(log n) time and O(1) space. Search on the answer makes O(log R) checks over a range of size R. The lower bound in JavaScript, which also solves search insert position:

[[code]]

steps.label: Name the question
steps.detail: Exact match, first true, last true, or smallest feasible answer?

steps.label: State the invariant
steps.detail: For example: the answer is in [lo, hi]

steps.label: Pick the matching template
steps.detail: Loop condition, updates and mid rounding go together

steps.label: Set bounds that include every answer
steps.detail: Insert position: hi = n. On the answer: hi surely works

steps.label: Test tiny inputs
steps.detail: Empty, one and two elements; target below, above and absent

activity.title: Search a rotated sorted array
activity.prompt: At each mid, decide which half is sorted with nums[lo] <= nums[mid], then check whether the target falls inside that half's range. Test a two-element array such as [3, 1] with target 1 before you submit.

check.question: You need the first day on which at least m bouquets can be made, and waiting more days never makes fewer bouquets possible. Which template fits?
choices: Exact match: while lo <= hi with lo = mid + 1 and hi = mid - 1, returning on equality
First true: while lo < hi, mid rounds down, hi = mid when feasible, otherwise lo = mid + 1
Last true: while lo < hi, mid rounds up, lo = mid when feasible
A linear scan over every day, because days are not an array
check.explanation: Feasibility is false, false, ..., true, true over the days, and you want the first true. That is the same template as lower bound and minimum printing speed. There is no exact value to match, and a linear scan over up to 10^9 days is too slow.

keyTerms.definition: Repeatedly halving a search range by asking a yes or no question at its middle; O(log n) steps.
A statement kept true by every update, such as "if present, the target is in nums[lo..hi]".
A yes or no question whose answer switches at most once over the range, such as false, false, true, true.
A range [lo, hi] that contains both ends, used by the exact-match template with while lo <= hi.
A range [lo, hi) that excludes hi, used by lower bound with hi starting at len(nums).
The first index whose value is at least the target; the insert position, as returned by bisect_left.
A sorted array shifted so it starts in the middle, made of two sorted runs, such as [4, 5, 6, 7, 0, 1, 2].
Searching a range of candidate answers with a monotonic feasibility check instead of searching an array.
mid = lo + (hi - lo) // 2, which avoids the overflow lo + hi can cause with fixed-width integers.

summary: Binary search needs a monotonic yes or no question; about 30 steps cover a billion items.
Inclusive: `hi = n - 1`, `while lo <= hi`, then `lo = mid + 1` or `hi = mid - 1`.
Lower bound: `hi = n`, `while lo < hi`, then `lo = mid + 1` or `hi = mid`.
Every step must shrink the range: `lo = mid` needs mid rounded up.
In a rotated array one half around mid is always sorted.
Search on the answer finds the smallest feasible value in O(log range) checks.
lesson.feynmanPrompt: Explain to a friend how you could find the slowest printer speed that still finishes every job on time by only asking "is this speed fast enough?", and why each answer lets you throw away half of the remaining speeds.

questions.question: At most about how many steps does binary search need for 1,000,000,000 sorted items? Answer with a whole number.
questions.explanation: 2^30 is about 1.07 billion, so about 30 halvings shrink a billion items to one. A linear scan could need a billion comparisons.

questions.question: What must be true for binary search to apply?
choices: The input must be an array of integers
There is a yes or no question whose answers switch from no to yes only once across the range
The input must contain no duplicates
The input size must be a power of two
questions.explanation: One test at the middle can only discard half the range if the answers are monotonic. Arrays of strings, duplicates and any length are fine, and with binary search on the answer there may be no array at all.

questions.question: Which of these can binary search solve efficiently? Select all that apply.
choices: Find the first occurrence of 7 in a sorted array with duplicates
Find the minimum of a rotated sorted array of distinct values
Find the smallest ship capacity that delivers all packages within D days
Find the most frequent value in an unsorted array
Find the integer square root of n
questions.explanation: Each of those has a monotonic question: is nums[i] >= 7, is nums[mid] > nums[hi], does capacity c work, is r * r > n. The most frequent value has no such ordering; it needs a counting map.

questions.question: What does it mean for a predicate to be monotonic, and why does binary search need it?
questions.answer: As x increases, the predicate switches from false to true at most once (false, ..., false, true, ..., true). Then one test at the middle tells you which side holds the switch, so the other half can be discarded.
questions.explanation: Without monotonicity, a false at mid says nothing about the other values, and you would have to check them all.

questions.question: Fill the blank with the overflow-safe midpoint that rounds down.
questions.explanation: hi - lo never overflows, and adding half of it to lo lands between them. lo + hi // 2 divides only hi because of operator precedence, (hi - lo) // 2 forgets to add lo, and / gives a float in Python 3.

questions.question: binary_search([2, 4, 6, 8, 10, 12], 10) uses the inclusive template. Which indexes does mid take, in order?
questions.explanation: lo = 0, hi = 5 gives mid = 2 (6 < 10), so lo = 3. lo = 3, hi = 5 gives mid = 4, which holds 10. Rounding down picks index 2 first, not 3.

questions.question: binary_search([1, 3], 5) never returns. Why?
choices: lo = mid does not move past mid, so when mid == lo the range never shrinks; use lo = mid + 1
The loop should be while lo < hi
It should return lo instead of -1
questions.explanation: lo = 0, hi = 1, mid = 0, and 1 < 5 sets lo = 0 again, forever. In the inclusive template mid has been checked, so both updates should skip it. Python integers cannot overflow.

questions.question: Why can (lo + hi) / 2 cause a bug in Java or C++ but not in Python?
choices: Python sorts the array before searching
Java and C++ cannot divide integers by 2
With fixed-width integers, lo + hi can overflow and become negative; Python integers grow as needed
Python division is slower, which hides the bug
questions.explanation: With 32-bit ints, two indexes above about 1.07 billion add up past the maximum and wrap to a negative number, giving an invalid index. lo + (hi - lo) / 2 avoids the large sum. Python's ints are arbitrary precision.

questions.question: What does this JavaScript log?
questions.code:
const nums = [1, 3, 5, 7]
const lo = 0
const hi = nums.length - 1
const mid = (lo + hi) / 2
console.log(mid, nums[mid])
questions.explanation: JavaScript's / does not round, so mid is 1.5, and nums[1.5] is undefined (no error). Use Math.floor((lo + hi) / 2) or lo + Math.floor((hi - lo) / 2).

questions.question: What does binary_search([1, 3, 5, 7, 9, 11, 13], 4) return with the inclusive template, which returns -1 when the target is absent?
questions.explanation: The range narrows around where 4 would be, between 3 and 5, until lo passes hi. The empty range means 4 is not present.

questions.question: What does lower_bound([1, 3, 3, 3, 5], 3) return (the first index whose value is at least 3)?
questions.explanation: Index 1 holds the first 3. Lower bound always lands on the first copy of a repeated value, which is why it finds first occurrences.

questions.question: What does bisect.bisect_right([1, 3, 3, 3, 5], 3) return?
questions.explanation: bisect_right returns the first position whose value is greater than 3, which is index 4 (the 5). Index 3 is the last 3, which is bisect_right - 1.

questions.question: Fill the blank so lower_bound can return len(nums) when every value is smaller than the target.
questions.explanation: The half-open range [0, n) leaves n as a possible answer, meaning "after the end". Starting at n - 1 makes that impossible, and n + 1 lets mid index past the array.

questions.question: In the half-open lower bound loop (while lo < hi, mid rounding down), why doesn't hi = mid cause an infinite loop?
choices: Because lo also moves on every iteration
Because the loop exits as soon as nums[mid] equals the target
It does loop forever on two-element arrays
mid rounds down and lo < hi, so mid < hi, and setting hi = mid always shrinks the range
questions.explanation: With lo < hi, lo + (hi - lo) // 2 is at most hi - 1. So hi = mid strictly decreases hi, and lo = mid + 1 strictly increases lo. The loop does not stop at equality; it keeps narrowing to the first match.

questions.question: How do you count how many times x appears in a sorted list in O(log n)?
questions.explanation: bisect_left is the first copy and bisect_right is just past the last copy, so their difference is the count, and it is 0 when x is absent. nums.count(x) is correct but O(n), and the reversed difference is negative.

questions.question: Put the steps of the half-open lower bound in order.
items: If nums[mid] < target set lo = mid + 1, otherwise set hi = mid
questions.explanation: The bounds include the after-the-end answer, the loop stops when the range is empty, and the updates keep the invariant: everything before lo is too small, everything from hi on is big enough.

questions.question: The loop is while lo < hi with mid = lo + (hi - lo) // 2. Which update pair can loop forever?
questions.explanation: Rounding down makes mid == lo on a two-element range, so lo = mid changes nothing. That pair needs mid to round up. The other pairs always move a bound past mid or onto a smaller mid.

questions.question: This finds the last index with nums[i] <= target (assuming nums[0] <= target). Fill the blank so it always terminates.
questions.explanation: lo = mid keeps mid, so mid must round up to guarantee progress. The two round-down choices make mid == lo on two elements and loop forever; hi - 1 gives a linear scan from the right.

questions.question: Match each binary search template with its updates.

pairs.right: lo = mid + 1 and hi = mid, mid rounds down
lo = mid and hi = mid - 1, mid rounds up

questions.explanation: These three combinations are the safe ones: each shrinks the range every iteration and keeps its invariant. Mixing parts of different rows is the most common source of binary search bugs.

questions.question: Which inputs are most worth tracing to catch off-by-one and infinite-loop bugs in a binary search? Select all that apply.
choices: A target smaller than every element
questions.explanation: Bugs live at the boundaries: empty ranges, ranges where lo == hi, the two-element case where rounding matters, and answers at the very ends. A large random array rarely exercises those paths.

questions.question: State the rule that guarantees a binary search loop terminates.
questions.answer: Every iteration must make the range strictly smaller. If an update keeps mid (lo = mid or hi = mid), round mid away from that side: round up when you write lo = mid, round down when you write hi = mid. If both updates skip mid, use while lo <= hi.
questions.explanation: Checking the two-element case against this rule catches nearly every infinite loop before you run the code.

questions.question: What does find_min([6, 7, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5]) return?
questions.explanation: The array is [1..7] rotated to start at 6. The minimum is at the drop from 7 to 1. In the search, mid = 3 (2 <= 5) sets hi = 3, mid = 1 (7 > 2) sets lo = 2, and mid = 2 (1 <= 2) sets hi = 2.

questions.question: In find_min for a rotated array, why compare nums[mid] with nums[hi] instead of nums[lo]?
choices: nums[lo] might be out of range
Comparing with lo makes the algorithm O(n)
Comparing with hi also handles an array that is not rotated, with no special case
questions.explanation: In a non-rotated array nums[mid] <= nums[hi] always holds, so hi keeps moving left to index 0, which is correct. Comparing with nums[lo] would see a sorted left half and wrongly search to the right of it.

questions.question: search([3, 1], 1) returns -1 instead of 1. What is the bug?
choices: The right-half check should be nums[mid] <= target
When lo == mid the left half is one sorted element, but < treats it as unsorted; use nums[lo] <= nums[mid]
The loop should be while lo < hi
questions.explanation: At lo = mid = 0, 3 < 3 is false, so the code assumes the right half (just index 0 here) is sorted, finds 1 outside [3, 3], and sets hi = -1. With <=, the left half counts as sorted, 1 is not in [3, 3), and lo moves to 1, where it finds the target.

questions.question: Why can duplicates push rotated-array search to O(n) in the worst case?
choices: When nums[lo], nums[mid] and nums[hi] are equal you cannot tell which half is sorted, so you may only shrink the range by one
Binary search cannot compare equal values
Duplicates double the length of the array
questions.explanation: In [1, 1, 1, 0, 1] or [1, 0, 1, 1, 1], the endpoints and mid all read 1, but the drop is on different sides. The safe move is to shrink one end by one, and an adversarial input forces that many times.

questions.question: Searching for 5 in [4, 5, 6, 7, 0, 1, 2]: lo = 0, hi = 6, mid = 3 (value 7). Which part is searched next?
choices: The left half, because it is sorted and 4 <= 5 < 7
questions.explanation: nums[0] = 4 <= nums[3] = 7, so the left half is sorted, and 5 lies in [4, 7), so hi = mid - 1. Comparing only with mid, as in plain binary search, would not be reliable in a rotated array.

questions.question: Jobs of [3, 6, 7, 11] pages, printing at most 5 pages per hour on one job at a time. How many hours does it take?
questions.explanation: ceil(3/5) + ceil(6/5) + ceil(7/5) + ceil(11/5) = 1 + 2 + 2 + 3 = 8. Each job's last partial hour still counts as a full hour.

questions.question: Jobs are [30, 11, 23, 4, 20] pages, and there are at least as many hours as jobs. What is the smallest search range that surely contains the minimum speed?
questions.explanation: Speed 1 is the slowest possible, and speed 30 (the largest job) finishes every job in one hour, which fits because hours >= jobs. 0 is not a valid speed, the answer could be below 4 when hours are plentiful, and 88 (the sum) is a valid but needlessly large upper bound.

questions.question: Fill the blank so the hours for a job of p pages at speed s use integer ceiling division.
questions.explanation: Adding s - 1 before floor division rounds any remainder up. p // s drops partial hours, p // s + 1 overcounts when s divides p exactly (6 pages at speed 3 would be 3 hours instead of 2), and (p - 1) // s undercounts.

questions.question: What is the time complexity of binary search on the answer for the printing problem, with n jobs and the largest job M pages?
questions.explanation: The search over speeds 1 to M makes O(log M) feasibility checks, and each check sums over n jobs. O(n M) is the linear scan over every speed.

questions.question: Jobs are [30, 11, 23, 4, 20] pages and there are 6 hours. What is the minimum speed?
questions.explanation: At 23 pages per hour the hours are 2 + 1 + 1 + 1 + 1 = 6, which fits. At 22, the 23-page job takes 2 hours as well, making 7. The binary search finds 23 in about 5 checks.

questions.question: You need the largest x for which cond(x) holds, and cond reads true, ..., true, false, ..., false. Which loop body is correct with while lo < hi?
choices: mid rounds up; lo = mid when cond(mid) holds, otherwise hi = mid - 1
mid rounds down; lo = mid + 1 when cond(mid) holds, otherwise hi = mid
mid rounds down; lo = mid when cond(mid) holds, otherwise hi = mid
mid rounds up; hi = mid when cond(mid) holds, otherwise lo = mid + 1
questions.explanation: A true mid might be the answer, so keep it with lo = mid, which requires rounding up to make progress. A false mid is excluded with hi = mid - 1. The second choice finds the first false instead, and the third can loop forever.

questions.question: search_insert([1, 3, 5, 6], 7) returns 3, but 7 belongs at index 4. What is wrong?
choices: nums[mid] < target should be nums[mid] <= target
The loop should be while lo <= hi
hi must start at len(nums), so the answer can be past the end
questions.explanation: With hi = 3, the range can never produce 4, so a target larger than everything stops at the last index. The half-open template starts with hi = len(nums).
